name: Fatima Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a full-stack developer at a small web agency, twelve of us, building online shops for local businesses: a bike shop, two butchers, a wool shop with a very particular owner. I use AI all day, for drafting product pages, writing tests and fixing my own typos in the code. I love the moment a shop owner sees their first online order come in. What wears me out is clients who want a website like Amazon's for the price of a takeaway.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house with three others, and I work weekend shifts at the climbing gym, mostly for the free climbing. My savings are under a month, mainly because I spent them on a trip to see my cousins in the summer, and I'd do it again. There aren't many developer jobs in this town, but I pick up small freelance sites, so I've never felt stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful, not magic, and that the people promising miracles were selling something. At work I'd say let's keep using what saves time. I'd probably post a short thread on what actually worked for us, with real examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd suit me fine. I'm already the fastest on the team because I use AI for the boring parts, so I'd keep that edge. Money's thin, but I've got the agency salary, the gym shifts and the odd freelance site, so I'm not worried week to week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and take on one more freelance shop a month, using AI to build it in a weekend. I'd rebuild some savings, maybe a month's rent by spring, mostly because my mum keeps asking. I'd keep the gym shifts because I love them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, honestly. A little disappointed that the exciting version didn't happen, but my life works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that could go wrong for you anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the high street keeps shrinking, our clients close. The wool shop owner told me last month her rent doubled. But I'd still find work, because a shop that survives needs a website more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does your mum ask about your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a nurse and she's saved ten percent of every pay cheque since she was nineteen. My mum thinks my climbing trips are a moral failing, and she's not entirely wrong.

say: I'd say AI tools are **useful, not magic**, and the miracle promisers were selling something.
I'd post a short **thread** on what actually worked for us, with real examples.
think: I'm already the **fastest on the team** because AI does my boring parts.
Money's thin, but the salary, **gym shifts** and freelance work cover each week.
do: Take on **one more freelance shop** a month, built in a weekend with AI.
Rebuild **a month's rent** in savings by spring.
feel: **Relaxed**, a little **disappointed** that the exciting version didn't happen.
S0.quote: My mum thinks my climbing trips are a moral failing, and she's not entirely wrong.
fieldNote: Despite **thin savings**, three income streams make her feel secure, so calm fits.
Her only real worry is **high street** decline, which she turns into opportunity.
Her mum's **saving habit** is a gentle foil to her own risk-taking.

steps.text: Keep building agency shop sites with AI drafting help
Take one extra freelance shop website each month
Save a month's rent by spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's the one I'd actually bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people need practical help, not lectures. At work I'd offer to show everyone the tools I use. Online I'd post honest notes on what's worth learning, because a lot of people would be lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out ahead for a few years. An agency of twelve might become eight, but the ones who can run AI well get busier. I'd feel bad for the others, but I'm not going to pretend I wouldn't be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up AI tools so we can build a shop in two days instead of two weeks, and pitch cheaper packages to the struggling shops on the high street. I'd start my own small freelance brand on the side, aiming for three regular clients by the end of the year. I'd keep a month's rent saved, no more trips until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a twinge of guilt. Being good with AI in a shrinking web agency is like being the only one who brought an umbrella.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the agency would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan, our designer, who still draws everything by hand first. He's lovely and slow. If the AI can make a decent design in a minute, I don't know how the boss justifies his salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does starting your own brand risk your job at the agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, if my boss sees it as competition. I'd only take clients the agency turns away, like tiny shops with no budget. I'd tell him straight, because he'd find out anyway in a town this size.

say: I'd say people need **practical help**, not lectures, to deal with this change.
I'd offer to show colleagues the **tools I use** every day.
think: I'd come out **ahead** for a few years, even if the agency drops from twelve to eight.
I'd feel **bad for others**, but I won't pretend I'd be in trouble.
do: Set up AI tools so the agency builds a shop in **two days**.
Pitch **cheaper packages** to struggling high street shops.
Start a **freelance brand** and win three regular clients this year.
feel: **Excited**, with a twinge of **guilt**, like the only one with an umbrella.
S1.quote: Being good with AI in a shrinking web agency is like being the only one who brought an umbrella.
fieldNote: She expects to **gain**, but sees colleagues like Dan losing out.
Her **freelance brand** is careful: only clients the agency turns away.
Her **guilt** is real but doesn't change her plans.

steps.text: Set up AI tools to build a client shop in two days
Launch a freelance web brand for tiny shops the agency refuses
Keep a month's rent saved and skip trips this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. That's a lot less fun than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and that the government needs a plan for income, fast. I'd still tell people to learn the tools, because being useful for even a year matters. I wouldn't do doom posting; I'd share practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my edge disappears. If AI can do any thinking job, a shop owner just asks it for a website and skips me. My whole job is screen work, so I'd be out within a year of 2028, maybe two if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop all trips and build three months of savings, because nothing else matters as much. I'd sell as many AI shop setups as I can before 2028, while people still need a human to do it. Then I'd ask the climbing gym about full-time work in route-setting and coaching, since robots come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I'm usually the calm one, and this would take that away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How realistic is the climbing gym as a living?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, honestly. Route-setters earn less than I do now, and there's one full-time spot at our gym. But it's hands-on and it's people, so it might buy me three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she was right about saving. She'd be kind about it, then make me a spreadsheet. I'd actually use it this time.

say: I'd say it's a **shock** and the government needs an **income plan** fast.
I'd keep telling people to **learn the tools**, because being useful for a year matters.
think: My **edge disappears** if a shop owner can just ask AI for a website.
My job is all **screen work**, so I'd expect to be out within a year or two of 2028.
do: Stop all trips and build **three months** of savings.
Sell as many **AI shop setups** as possible before 2028.
Ask the climbing gym about **route-setting** and coaching work.
feel: **Shaken**, losing her usual sense of being **the calm one**.
S2.quote: If AI can do any thinking job, a shop owner just asks it for a website and skips me.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** stops protecting her here, and she says so.
The **climbing gym** is a modest, honest fallback that she doesn't oversell.
She'd finally take her **mum's advice** on saving.

steps.text: Stop travel and save three months of rent
Sell AI online shop setups to local businesses before 2028
Apply for route-setting and coaching work at the climbing gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but not a lot, and people should start now. I'd run free evening sessions for small shop owners on using AI, because they'll need it. I'd say employers should be honest with staff about timelines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I get a good three years out of being the AI person. After that, websites basically build themselves. I'd need to be doing something else by 2031, and I don't know what that is yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For three years I'd grow my freelance side into a proper small business helping local shops run their whole online side with AI. I'd save hard, aiming for six months by 2029. And I'd do a coaching qualification at the climbing gym, as a backup that's hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but motivated. It's a deadline, and I'm better with deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't the business doomed in 2031 too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the website part, yes. But shop owners might still want someone they trust to set it up and fix it when it goes weird. For a local shop owner, the trust part lasts longer than the coding part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in this town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. The shops I'd work with are here, and so is the gym. Moving to the city just means more competition for the same disappearing jobs.

say: I'd say there's time, but **not a lot**, and people should start now.
I'd run **free evening sessions** for small shop owners on using AI.
think: I get about **three good years** as the AI person, then websites build themselves.
I need to be doing **something else** by 2031, and I don't know what yet.
do: Grow freelancing into a **small business** running local shops' online side with AI.
Get a **coaching qualification** at the climbing gym as a hands-on backup.
feel: **Nervous** but **motivated**, because she works better with deadlines.
S3.quote: For a local shop owner, the trust part lasts longer than the coding part.
fieldNote: She expects her developer work to fade by 2031, so this is **anxious**, not uneasy.
Her bet is on **trust** with local shop owners outlasting the coding.
She'd **stay local**, seeing the city as more competition, not more safety.

steps.text: Turn freelance work into a small business for local shops
Save six months of costs by 2029
Earn a climbing coaching qualification at the gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's practically forever in tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, so people shouldn't panic, but they shouldn't sleep on it. I'd tell schools to teach practical skills alongside coding. I'd keep sharing what I learn online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the next five years are great for me. I'd be the person local shops call, and the agency would need me. The question is what I'm doing in my late thirties, and I'd have time to figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my own small business slowly over five years and stay at the agency until it's paying my rent. I'd learn whatever AI tools come next, as early as I can. And I'd finally save properly, three months by year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small worry sitting in the back. Ten years is enough time to be curious instead of scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could make this go badly for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I get comfortable. I've watched people coast on one skill for years. With a decade, the risk is thinking there's always next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. I'd still travel and climb. I'd maybe save for a flat deposit, which I've never thought about before.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to plan properly, without panic or sleepwalking.
I'd tell schools to teach **practical skills** alongside coding.
think: The **next five years** look great for me as the person local shops call.
My **late thirties** are the question, and I'd have time to work it out.
do: Build a **small business** slowly while staying at the agency until it pays the rent.
Learn each new **AI tool** as early as possible.
Save **three months** of costs by year two.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with a **small worry** at the back.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to be curious instead of scared.
fieldNote: With a decade, her own job and side work feel **secure**, so calm fits.
She names **complacency** as her main risk, an honest self-check.
She'd consider a **flat deposit** for the first time.

steps.text: Grow a small web business slowly over five years
Learn each new AI building tool as it appears
Save three months of costs by year two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the thing I'm good at before I've built anything else. What would help is a basic income floor for a couple of years, and grants for small businesses run by people who lost their jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small shops. Everyone talks about big tech and big companies, but the wool shop and the butcher are where people like me actually make a living.

headlineQuote: The wool shop and the butcher are where people like me actually make a living.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old** full-stack developer building online shops for local businesses.
She rents a room in a **shared house** and works weekend shifts at a climbing gym.
She uses AI **all day** and expects to come out ahead in slower change.
Her calm breaks with **AGI by 2028**, when shop owners could skip her entirely.
Her plan is a small business built on **trust** with local shops, plus climbing coaching.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which takes away her skill before she has built anything else.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** floor for a couple of years.
**Grants** for small businesses started by people who lost jobs.
